Concretely: begin the day with his word and with prayer, not as a duty to tick but as a man taking in food; remind yourself of what grace has already done (forgiven, adopted, sealed); confess sin quickly so that nothing stands between you and the supply; and receive the means he has given, the preaching of the word, the Lord’s Supper and the fellowship of believers. Grace does not usually feel like a surge of power. It feels like being able to do the next right thing, and then the next.

I am not a teacher. Does verse 2 involve me? Yes, in two ways. First, the church needs faithful people to entrust the gospel to, and faithfulness is something any believer can be: you can pray for those who teach, support their training, and test what you hear. Second, the chain runs through ordinary relationships too. Parents teach children, older women train younger women (Titus 2:3–5), and friends explain the gospel to friends. The office of teaching in the church belongs to qualified men, the elders; but the duty of passing on what you have received belongs to every Christian. Someone handed it to you. Think whom you could hand it to.

In a sentence. As for you, my son, keep drawing your strength from the grace that is in Christ Jesus. What you heard from me, confirmed by many witnesses, hand on to trustworthy people who will be competent to teach others too.

On a Tuesday. Who are you training to know and teach the faith? Think of one person you could invest in this year: read a book of the Bible with them, meet regularly, pray together. Then thank God by name for the people who did that for you.

For worship. The risen Christ entrusted his gospel to fishermen and a converted persecutor, and he has never once let the chain break. Empires have fallen, churches have been burned, and the word has passed from hand to hand across twenty centuries until it reached yours. The grace that kept Paul in his cell keeps every faithful teacher today, and the Lord who gives the gifts also supplies the strength to use them. Glory to the Lord of the harvest, who is building his church through ordinary, reliable people, and who has promised that the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.

verseByVerse.quote: Share in suffering as a good soldier of Christ Jesus. No soldier gets entangled in civilian pursuits, since his aim is to please the one who enlisted him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Share in suffering as a good soldier of Christ Jesus. No soldier gets entangled in civilian pursuits, since his aim is to please the one who enlisted him.

Share in suffering. The same compound verb as 1:8 (synkakopathēson): suffer together with. Suffering for the gospel is shared, and this is the first of three images that follow in quick succession.

As a good soldier of Christ Jesus. “Soldier” (stratiōtēs). Roman soldiers endured hard training, long marches, poor food and danger, and the Christian worker must expect the same (Philippians 2:25; Philemon 2). “Good” (kalos) is noble, fine. The soldier is chosen for a specific quality, and Paul names it in the next clause.

No soldier gets entangled in civilian pursuits. “Entangled” (empleketai) means woven into, caught up as in a net, and “civilian pursuits” (tais tou biou pragmateiais) are literally the affairs of life: not sinful things but ordinary ones, business, property, domestic arrangements. Roman soldiers on active service were forbidden to trade or farm; they had to be ready to fight. Paul is not saying a soldier must have no life. A man on active service has accepted a limit on how much of ordinary life he can carry, because he can be moved at any hour.

Since his aim is to please the one who enlisted him. “Enlisted” (stratologēsanti) is recruited, enrolled as a soldier. Christ enlisted us; we did not volunteer him. And he enlisted us at a price: we are not our own, for we were bought (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). Our aim is to please him, not ourselves or others (2 Corinthians 5:9; Galatians 1:10). He has exactly one person to satisfy, which simplifies a great many decisions and rules out a great many others. Applied to Timothy, in a church full of people with opinions about him, this is a considerable relief. He is not required to satisfy the congregation, the older men who resent him, or the teachers he is opposing. One audience, one commanding officer.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ministers may never work at a trade; Paul himself made tents (Acts 18:3). The point is not being entangled: allowing ordinary affairs to become a distraction from the main task. Nor does it make ordinary work unspiritual for other Christians. And it should be read with care rather than as a charter for neglect. Paul has just spent a letter insisting that a man manage his own household well and provide for his relatives (1 Timothy 3:4; 5:8). The soldier image is not permission to abandon ordinary duties; it is a warning against being so woven into comfort and property that you cannot be moved when the order comes.

How do I know whether something is an entanglement? Ask three questions. Does it compete with Christ for my first loyalty, so that I find myself pleasing it, or the people attached to it, rather than him? Does it make me unavailable for what he clearly asks, so that I cannot serve, give, or move because I am tied up? And would I be willing to put it down tomorrow if he required it? Good things become entanglements by growth, not by nature: the second job, the house project, the hobby, the online world. Your family is not an entanglement; it is a calling (1 Timothy 5:8). But even good duties need to be carried in a way that leaves you a soldier, not a civilian.

In a sentence. Take your share of hardship like a good soldier of Christ Jesus. No soldier on duty gets tangled up in everyday business, because he wants to please the officer who enlisted him.

On a Tuesday. What is entangling you, distracting you from Christ’s calling? Identify it and loosen its grip this week: a subscription cancelled, a commitment declined, an evening given back. And when you face a decision this week, ask simply: which choice would please the one who enlisted me?

For worship. Our captain did not stay behind the lines. The Son of God laid aside the glory of heaven, entangled himself in nothing that would turn him from his Father’s will, set his face like flint toward Jerusalem, and endured the cross for the joy set before him. He enlisted us not because we were promising recruits but because he had already won the war. To please him is not a burden but the freedom of belonging to the best of masters, whose yoke is easy and whose burden is light.

verseByVerse.quote: An athlete is not crowned unless he competes according to the rules. It is the hard-working farmer who ought to have the first share of the crops. Think over what I say, for the Lord will give you understanding in everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An athlete is not crowned unless he competes according to the rules. It is the hard-working farmer who ought to have the first share of the crops. Think over what I say, for the Lord will give you understanding in everything.

An athlete is not crowned unless he competes according to the rules. The crown (stephanoutai) is the victor’s wreath, and the condition is exact: lawfully (nomimōs), by the rules, which in the Greek games included the required months of training as well as the contest. At Olympia athletes swore they had trained for ten months and would keep the rules, and a man could win the race and be disqualified for what he did beforehand. Effort alone qualifies nobody. There is a right way to do this work, holiness, truth, endurance, and energy spent outside it earns nothing.

The crown without the cross refused. The athlete’s temptation, to take the crown by some other route, was offered once to Christ himself in its purest form. The devil showed him all the kingdoms of the world and offered them for a single act of worship (Matthew 4:8–10): the crown without the cross. Jesus refused, and ran the course his Father set, through Gethsemane and Golgotha, and he is now crowned with glory and honour because he suffered death (Hebrews 2:9). Every shortcut in ministry is a small echo of that offer. And the crown Timothy runs for will be given by the Lord who ran first and kept every rule (4:8).

It is the hard-working farmer who ought to have the first share of the crops. The adjective is the labouring word, kopiōnta, work to exhaustion. And the farmer adds what the other two lack: time. A soldier’s engagement is decided in a day, an athlete’s in an afternoon; a farmer works for months and sees nothing, and if he stops there will be no harvest. Ministry is like that: hard, often unseen, slow-growing work, but there will be fruit, and the worker will share in it, in this life (1 Corinthians 9:7–11) and in the next.

Think over what I say. It is a small masterpiece of teaching method. “Think over” (noei) is consider, reflect on, understand. Paul does not explain the three pictures. He hands them over and tells Timothy to work at them.

For the Lord will give you understanding in everything. And then he promises that the understanding (synesis, insight, comprehension) will be given. Both halves are there and neither cancels the other. Hard thinking is commanded; illumination is God’s gift (Proverbs 2:1–6; James 1:5). The man who waits for insight without labouring will not get it, and the man who labours as though it depends on his own cleverness has misunderstood where it comes from.

What it does not mean. The athlete’s crown does not mean we earn salvation by keeping rules. The crown is the reward God graciously gives to faithful service (4:8; 1 Corinthians 9:25). Nor does the farmer’s share mean ministry is about financial gain.

What if I have worked for years and seen no fruit? Then you are a farmer in the long months, and this verse is for you. Fruit in God’s work is often invisible, delayed, or harvested by someone else: one sows and another reaps (John 4:37–38). Faithfulness is your responsibility; growth is God’s (1 Corinthians 3:6–7). Check honestly that you are competing by the rules, that the seed is the word of God and the method is not compromise. Then keep sowing, and leave the calendar to him. Many a missionary has died before the church he planted grew, and many a mother never saw the prayer for her son answered in her lifetime. Your labour in the Lord is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58).

How do I think over Scripture? Read a passage slowly, more than once. Ask what it says, what it meant to the first readers, and what it shows about God and about Christ. Notice the images and the connecting words, therefore, but, for. Write down a sentence summarising it, and one way it touches your life. Pray before and after, asking the Lord for the understanding he promises. Carry a verse with you through the day and turn it over, the way a cow chews the cud. Use good helps, a sound commentary, your pastor’s preaching, but do not let them do all the thinking for you.

In a sentence. An athlete wins the prize only if he competes by the rules. The farmer who has done the hard work should be the first to enjoy the harvest. Think about what I am saying, and the Lord will give you insight into all of it.

On a Tuesday. Your work for Christ may feel slow and unseen: the Sunday school class, the prayer meeting, the child who does not listen, the neighbour who never comes. Keep going: the harvest is coming. And this week take one of these three pictures and think it over for ten minutes, asking the Lord what it means for you.

For worship. The Lord is the God of the long harvest. He waited long ages for the fullness of time, and then sent his Son as a seed into the ground: unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone, but if it dies, it bears much fruit (John 12:24). That one seed has become a harvest no one can number. He gives the crown to those who run, the share to those who labour, and the understanding to those who ask. Blessed be the Lord of the harvest, who is never in a hurry and never late.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, the offspring of David, as preached in my gospel, for which I am suffering, bound with chains as a criminal. But the word of God is not bound!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, the offspring of David, as preached in my gospel, for which I am suffering, bound with chains as a criminal. But the word of God is not bound!

Remember Jesus Christ. “Remember” (mnēmoneue) is present tense: keep remembering, keep him in view. Paul does not tell Timothy to work something out or achieve something. Under pressure the things you know perfectly well stop being present to you, and the remedy is recollection. It is what the Lord’s Supper is for: do this in remembrance of me. In hardship, the greatest encouragement is not a technique but a person.

Risen from the dead. The participle (egēgermenon) is perfect: having been raised, and remaining so. Not an event in the past that occurred and finished, but a standing condition. There is a risen man. He is not a dead hero but a living Lord. For a man facing execution, and for Timothy facing danger, the resurrection is everything. Death is not the end.

The offspring of David. Literally of David’s seed (ek spermatos Dauid). Two clauses, and they are the whole gospel in shorthand. Risen: so he is Lord and death is beaten. Offspring of David: so he is genuinely human, the promised Messianic King, and the promises to Israel have been kept in him (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Romans 1:3–4). The resurrection declares him to be the Son of God; his descent from David shows he is the promised King and truly human. Both together form the heart of the gospel. This also counters the false teachers, who perhaps downplayed his true humanity and, as verse 18 shows, the bodily resurrection. And this is the gospel Paul calls his own: not a rival version, but the gospel committed to him and preached by him (Romans 2:16; 16:25; 1 Timothy 1:11).

For which I am suffering, bound with chains as a criminal. “Criminal” (kakourgos) is evildoer, a malefactor, the same term Luke uses of the two men crucified beside Jesus (Luke 23:32–33). Paul is treated like a common criminal, not merely a political prisoner. He is classified with the worst, and so was his Lord.

But the word of God is not bound! Here is the sentence that lifts the paragraph off the page. The exclamation is in the Greek. Paul is chained (dedetai); the word is not. Rome can hold the apostle and can do nothing whatever to the message. It goes on spreading through others, through Paul’s letters, through those who visit him (Philippians 1:12–14). No prison can hold God’s word (Isaiah 55:11). And the proof is in your hands: the sentence written in that cell has travelled further than any of the men who put him there. Preachers can be silenced, buildings closed, Bibles confiscated; the word itself has never yet been imprisoned by anybody.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s suffering was pointless or that God was absent. God was working through it.

How do I remember Jesus Christ in practice? By deliberately bringing him to mind, especially when pressure makes you forget. Read the Gospels regularly, so that your picture of him is filled from Scripture and not from your moods. Come to the Lord’s Supper as a remembrance, not a ritual. Sing about him. When you are anxious, say to yourself the two facts of this verse: he is risen, so death and evil do not have the last word; he is David’s son, so every promise of God has come true in him (2 Corinthians 1:20). Remembering is not nostalgia. It is letting the facts of the gospel rearrange the facts of today.

In a sentence. Keep remembering Jesus Christ, raised from the dead, a descendant of David: that is my gospel, and for it I am suffering, even being chained like a criminal. But God’s word is not in chains!

On a Tuesday. When your situation feels like a cell, a diagnosis, a job you cannot leave, a home where you cannot speak freely, remember that the word of God is not bound there either. Pray for believers in prison for their faith today, by name if you can, and for the word to run freely where they are.

For worship. Jesus Christ is risen from the dead, and nothing will ever make him unrisen. The son of David sits on the throne promised to his father, and his kingdom has no end. The chains that held Paul are dust, Nero is a name in a history book, and the word Paul wrote from the cell is read in a thousand languages every day. He is the crucified criminal who is the King, the buried man who is the living Lord. Glory to the God whose word runs swiftly, and whom no prison on earth has ever held.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I endure everything for the sake of the elect, that they also may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus with eternal glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore I endure everything for the sake of the elect, that they also may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus with eternal glory.

Therefore I endure everything. “Therefore”: because the word is not bound, Paul’s suffering is worth it. “Endure” (hypomenō) means to remain under a weight without buckling. And “everything” is not rhetoric from this man. He has the list elsewhere: floggings, stonings, shipwrecks, hunger (2 Corinthians 11:23–28), and now chains, loneliness, cold (4:13), betrayal and approaching death.

For the sake of the elect. Note the reason. Not his own reward, but the elect: people, most of whom he has never met and some not yet born. His suffering is not merely borne; it is spent on somebody. “The elect” (tous eklektous) are those whom God chose before time began (1:9; Ephesians 1:4), including those not yet converted, whom God will call through the gospel. Paul does not know who they are, but he knows they exist, and so he knows his suffering will not be in vain.

That they also may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus. If God has chosen a people, why endure anything? Paul answers by what he does. “Obtain” (tychōsin) is attain, reach. Election has never in Scripture been a reason for inaction; it is the reason action is worth taking. God ordains both the end, salvation, and the means: preaching, suffering, prayer. Because Paul knows God has chosen people, his labour is not a gamble; because he does not know who they are, he preaches to everyone and endures anything to reach them. Certainty about the outcome produces energy, not idleness. It was the same logic that kept him in Corinth, when the Lord told him he had many people in that city (Acts 18:9–10).

Other sheep I have. Paul’s confidence about people he has never met is borrowed from his Lord. Jesus said that he had other sheep not yet in the fold, that he must bring them also, and that they would listen to his voice (John 10:16). The elect are first of all Christ’s: chosen in him before the ages began (1:9), and the salvation they obtain is in Christ Jesus and nowhere else. The Shepherd laid down his life for those sheep before most of them were born, and he gathers them now by the voice of his gospel in the mouths of men like Paul. That is why Paul’s suffering is never wasted. It carries the Shepherd’s own voice, and his sheep will hear it.

With eternal glory. The last words of the verse set the whole thing in proportion. Everything endured is weighed against what it purchases, and the purchase is not temporary. Salvation includes final glory, sharing in Christ’s glory for ever (Romans 8:17–18, 30), and this light momentary affliction is preparing an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison (2 Corinthians 4:17).

What it does not mean. It does not mean election makes evangelism pointless. Election is the reason evangelism will succeed. Nor does it mean Paul’s suffering atones for anyone; Christ alone saves. Paul’s suffering is the cost of bringing the message.

Does election mean someone might want to be saved and be turned away? No. Scripture never pictures a person longing for Christ and being refused because he was not chosen. The invitation is genuine and universal: whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37), and everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved (Romans 10:13). By nature no one seeks God (Romans 3:11); where a real desire for Christ appears, it is itself the sign that God is drawing that person. Election is not a wall keeping seekers out. It is the reason there are any seekers at all. So preach freely to everyone, and if you are wanting Christ, come.

Why should I put up with hardship for people I do not know? Because Christ did, and because they are his. Paul endured for people he had never met because he loved the Lord who had chosen them, and because he knew the gospel would reach them only if someone carried it. That is the logic of every missionary, every faithful Sunday school teacher, every believer who gives sacrificially to send the word to places he will never see. The hardship may be small: an awkward conversation, money you would rather keep, time with a difficult person. But it is never wasted, because somewhere on the other end of it is someone God has chosen and is calling.

In a sentence. That is why I put up with everything for the sake of God’s chosen people, so that they too may receive the salvation that is in Christ Jesus, together with eternal glory.

On a Tuesday. Share the gospel with confidence: God has chosen people who will respond. Your effort is never in vain. Pray this week for one unbeliever by name, asking God to call them, and look for one opportunity to speak to them of Christ.

For worship. Before the world began the Father wrote names in the Lamb’s book of life, and not one of those names will be missing on the last day. The Son endured the cross for the joy set before him, the joy of a people redeemed, and he endures still in the long patience of his gospel going out to the ends of the earth. Every hardship borne by his servants is caught up in that purpose. Blessed be the electing God, who chose a people, gave his Son to die for them, and will bring every one of them home with eternal glory.

verseByVerse.quote: The saying is trustworthy, for: If we have died with him, we will also live with him; if we endure, we will also reign with him; if we deny him, he also will deny us; if we are faithless, he remains faithful— for he cannot deny himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The saying is trustworthy, for: If we have died with him, we will also live with him; if we endure, we will also reign with him; if we deny him, he also will deny us; if we are faithless, he remains faithful— for he cannot deny himself.

The saying is trustworthy. The fourth of the five trustworthy sayings (1 Timothy 1:15; 3:1; 4:9; Titus 3:8). What follows has the balance and rhythm of a hymn: four conditional lines, perhaps sung in worship or used as a baptismal confession. And they do not all run the same way.

If we have died with him, we will also live with him. “Died with” (synapethanomen) is an aorist: died together with, at a point in the past. This happened at conversion, in union with Christ. It refers to our union with him in his death, which takes place when we come to faith and is signified in baptism (Romans 6:3–8; Colossians 3:3). It may also include martyrdom, and Paul is writing on the eve of his own. The dying is behind; the living is certain, now in new life and for ever in resurrection.

If we endure, we will also reign with him. Present and continuing: “endure” (hypomenomen) is keep on enduring, the word from verse 10, remaining under weight. And the promise attached is startlingly large: not merely survival but reigning (symbasileusomen). Those who suffer with Christ will share his kingdom (Romans 8:17; Revelation 3:21; 20:4–6).

If we deny him, he also will deny us. Then the line turns dark. “Deny” (arnēsometha) is disown, reject, renounce. It is the Lord’s own word: whoever denies me before men, I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven (Matthew 10:33). And it is not softened here. This is not a temporary failure under pressure, as with Peter, who repented, but a settled, final rejection of Christ. Settled, final denial has a settled, final answer: those who finally reject Christ will be rejected by him.

If we are faithless, he remains faithful. Here is the fourth line, and it is the reason this hymn is loved. Read carefully, because the pattern breaks. The first three lines match our action with a corresponding response. The fourth does not. We might expect: he will be faithless to us. Instead, we are faithless (apistoumen, unfaithful, lacking faith), and he remains faithful. The symmetry fails, and it fails in our favour. Our weakness, wavering and failures do not change his faithfulness to his promises and his people.

For he cannot deny himself. And the ground of the fourth line is not our sincerity but Christ’s nature. His faithfulness is not a policy he might revise. To abandon his people or break his promises would be to deny himself, to act contrary to his nature, and that is the one thing he cannot do (Numbers 23:19; Titus 1:2; Hebrews 6:18). Written to a frightened man by a dying one, it is the most reassuring sentence in the letter.

Denying and failing. How does the fourth line sit with the third? The distinction is between denying and failing. To deny is to repudiate, to disown deliberately and finally. To be faithless is to fail, to let him down, to be the sort of Christian who keeps collapsing. Peter did both kinds of thing on the same night: he denied, and it was faithlessness under fear, and the difference between him and Judas was not the size of the failure but what happened afterwards. Jesus had prayed for Peter that his faith would not fail (Luke 22:31–32), and it did not.

Where Christians differ: if Christ remains faithful, can a believer still be denied? Some take the third and fourth lines as contradictory: either believers can be lost (line three), or not (line four). Arminian Christians read the third line as a warning that real believers may fall away. Others take the fourth line as a threat: he remains faithful to his warnings and will judge the faithless. Verdict: Line three describes final, deliberate apostasy, which reveals that a person never truly belonged to Christ (1 John 2:19); such people will be disowned. Line four describes the weakness of genuine believers, who sometimes falter, doubt or fail, like Peter. Christ’s faithfulness to them does not depend on their strength; he keeps them, and so they do not finally deny him (John 10:28–29; Luke 22:31–32). The warning is real, and it is one of the means by which Christ keeps his people from apostasy; the comfort is real, and it is the ground of their perseverance.

What it does not mean. It does not mean any momentary failure or doubt brings condemnation. Peter denied Christ three times and was restored (John 21:15–19). Nor does it mean Christ is indifferent to unfaithfulness; he disciplines his own (Hebrews 12:5–11).

I once denied Christ, or hid my faith, when I was afraid. Am I lost? If you are troubled by it now, that is very strong evidence that you are not. The denial this verse warns about is a settled, final repudiation, the kind that does not grieve and does not return. Peter swore he did not know Jesus, and within weeks he was preaching at Pentecost. What you do is what Peter did: weep over it, confess it plainly to the Lord, and come back. Jesus met Peter on the shore with a fire and breakfast and asked him three times, do you love me (John 21:15–17), one question for each denial. He has not changed. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us (1 John 1:9).

What does it mean that we will reign with him? It means sharing in Christ’s rule as his people. In part this is already true: believers are seated with Christ in the heavenly places (Ephesians 2:6), and the souls of the martyrs reign with him now while they wait for the resurrection (Revelation 20:4). Its fullness comes at his return, when his people inherit the new creation and share in his kingdom for ever (Matthew 25:34; Revelation 22:5). It is not a reward for being impressive; it is the destiny of those united to the King. The servants who suffer with him now will be honoured with him then, and the reversal will be complete.

In a sentence. Here is a saying you can rely on: if we died with him, we shall also live with him; if we keep enduring, we shall also reign with him; if we disown him, he too will disown us; if we are unfaithful, he stays faithful, because he cannot be untrue to himself.

On a Tuesday. When you have failed him again this week, and you will, do not conclude that he has given up on you. Say the fourth line to yourself, and then get up and go on. And when you are tempted to soften your loyalty to him to avoid trouble, say the third line, and let the warning keep you.

For worship. Here is the steadiness of the Son of God. We are brave on Sunday and silent on Monday, fervent in the morning and cold by night, and through every failure he stays exactly what he has always been. He died, and we died in him; he lives, and our life is hidden with him; he reigns, and the throne he will share with his people is already prepared. Our grip on him slackens a hundred times, and his grip on us never once. Blessed be the faithful Christ, who keeps his word when we break ours, and who would have to stop being himself before he could let us go.
verseByVerse.note: The fourth of the “trustworthy sayings,” perhaps an early hymn.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–26 — A Worker Approved by God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Timothy must keep warning the church, before God, against quarrelling over words, which ruins those who listen. He should work to be a worker God approves, unashamed, teaching the message of truth accurately, and avoid empty, irreverent talk, which spreads like an infection; Hymenaeus and Philetus, for instance, are upsetting people’s faith by claiming the resurrection has already happened. Still, God’s foundation stands firm, sealed with two truths: the Lord knows his own, and those who call on his name must turn from evil. Like household utensils, people can be fit for honourable use if they cleanse themselves. Timothy should run from youthful desires and pursue righteousness, faith, love and peace with sincere believers, and refuse foolish arguments. The Lord’s servant must not fight but be kind, able to teach and patient, gently correcting opponents in the hope that God will grant them repentance and they will escape the devil’s snare.
verseByVerse.theology:
Cutting Straight

‘Rightly handling’ (v.15) is to cut straight, like a craftsman whose cut cannot be undone: accuracy, not eloquence. And God's foundation bears two seals (v.19) — the Lord knows his own, and those who name him depart from iniquity.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Hymenaeus, already disciplined (1 Tim 1:20), was still teaching that the resurrection had come — wrecking the hope of the grieving first.

Now: Word-fights damage the hearers (v.14); cleanse yourself rather than audit the house (v.21); and correct with gentleness, since repentance is God's to grant (v.25).

verseByVerse.quote: Remind them of these things, and charge them before God not to quarrel about words, which does no good, but only ruins the hearers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remind them of these things, and charge them before God not to quarrel about words, which does no good, but only ruins the hearers.

Remind them of these things. “Remind” (hypomimnēske) is present tense: keep reminding. “Them” are the faithful men (v. 2) and the church. “These things” are the truths of verses 1–13. Much of ministry is reminding people of what they already know (2 Peter 1:12–13).

And charge them before God. “Charge” (diamartyromenos) is solemnly warn, testify earnestly. Note the solemnity: before God, who sees and judges. This is the oath language of 1 Timothy 5:21 and 2 Timothy 4:1. Paul does not treat quarrelling about words as a minor irritation to be managed. He puts the congregation under oath about it.

Not to quarrel about words. The verb is logomachein, literally to word-fight, to battle over terms. It is the same disease diagnosed at Ephesus in the first letter (1 Timothy 6:4): arguments over trivial distinctions, word games and speculative points. Paul has been dealing with it for years and it has not gone away.

Which does no good, but only ruins the hearers. Then the verdict, in two parts. It does no good (ep’ ouden chrēsimon): literally it is useful for nothing, profitable in no respect. Whatever else may be said for a theological argument conducted this way, nobody is better for it. And it ruins the hearers. The word is katastrophē, overturning, subversion, the collapse of a structure; it gives us our word catastrophe. Such quarrels do not merely waste time; they damage faith.

The audience takes the damage. Notice who suffers: not the combatants, who are usually enjoying themselves, but the hearers, the people in the room who did not want the fight and have to watch it. Somebody sitting there is new in the faith, or barely holding on, and what they learn is that Christianity is a thing people shout about. The participants go home invigorated; something in the hearers has come down. Set against it is verse 15’s alternative: not quarrelling about the word, but rightly handling it.

The hearers Christ guards. On this point Paul has his Lord’s own warning behind him: whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in him to stumble would be better off drowned in the depths of the sea (Matthew 18:6). Jesus watched over the onlookers in his own debates. When the Sadducees brought him a trick question about a woman married seven times, he did not play their word game; he took them back to the Scriptures and the power of God, and showed them the living God of Abraham (Matthew 22:23–33). The crowd went away astonished at his teaching, not worn out by a quarrel. That is the alternative to word-fighting: an answer that leaves the listeners seeing God more clearly.

What it does not mean. It does not mean words do not matter or that doctrine is unimportant. Precise words matter greatly (v. 15). The problem is quarrelling over words in a way that serves pride and controversy rather than truth.

How do I tell a word-fight from a necessary argument for the truth? Look at the subject, the spirit and the fruit. The subject: is this about the gospel and what Scripture clearly teaches, or about a speculation, a label, or a point Scripture leaves open? The spirit: am I trying to help someone see the truth, or to win, to be seen winning, or to vent? Would I be as eager if no one were watching? The fruit: is anyone being built up, or are people being unsettled and divided? Paul himself argued hard for justification by faith (Galatians 2:11–14) and for the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15). Contending for the faith is right (Jude 3). Fighting about words for the pleasure of fighting is not.

In a sentence. Keep reminding people of these things, and warn them solemnly before God not to fight over words. It does no good and only wrecks the faith of those who listen.

On a Tuesday. Before you join an online theological argument, ask: will this build up or tear down those who are listening? Picture the quiet reader who never comments. If you must write, write as though that person were the one you were answering. And if a conversation at church is becoming a contest, change the subject to Christ, or end it kindly.

For worship. The Word who became flesh did not come to win arguments but to save sinners. He answered his enemies with truth and his weak disciples with patience; he did not quarrel or cry aloud, and he would not break a bruised reed (Matthew 12:19–20). His words are spirit and life, and every word of God proves true. Blessed be the Lord whose speech builds up, whose truth heals rather than wounds, and whose voice will still be speaking when every quarrel has fallen silent.

verseByVerse.quote: Do your best to present yourself to God as one approved, a worker who has no need to be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do your best to present yourself to God as one approved, a worker who has no need to be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth.

Do your best to present yourself to God as one approved. “Do your best” (spoudason) means be eager, make every effort, be diligent; the KJV renders it study, and ministry of the word requires hard work. “Present” (parastēsai) is to stand before, to offer. And the audience is named at once. Not the congregation, not the critics in Ephesus: to God. Timothy must seek God’s approval, not the crowd’s. “Approved” (dokimos) is the assayer’s word for metal that has been tested and passed as pure. It is a standing image of this correspondence (1 Timothy 3:10), and it implies that the test is real.

A worker who has no need to be ashamed. “Worker” (ergatēs) is a labourer; ministry is a craft. And “no need to be ashamed” (anepaischyntos) is the chapter-one word turned inside out: Timothy must not be ashamed of the gospel, and he must work so that his own labour gives him nothing to be ashamed of, like a craftsman whose work, when inspected, holds up.

Rightly handling the word of truth. Here is the phrase everything turns on. The Greek is orthotomeō, literally to cut straight, used in the Greek Old Testament of a straight path (Proverbs 3:6), and of a road cut straight or a furrow ploughed true. Paul was a tentmaker (Acts 18:3), and anyone who has cut cloth or hide knows that the material is expensive and a crooked cut cannot be uncut. The idea is accuracy: interpreting God’s word correctly and teaching it faithfully, so that people are led straight. “The word of truth” is the gospel and the whole of Scripture.

Accuracy, not eloquence. So the work Paul commends is not enthusiasm or eloquence but accuracy: giving what is actually there rather than what the preacher would like to be there. The word-fighters use Scripture as ammunition; the approved worker handles it like a man who will answer for every cut.

Where the straight cut leads. The word of truth is, in Paul’s own phrase, the gospel of your salvation (Ephesians 1:13), and that tells the workman where every straight cut ends. Jesus said of the Scriptures, it is they that bear witness about me (John 5:39). A crooked handling of the Bible is one that never arrives at him, or arrives only by forcing the text. Paul is not asking for clever links but for the real line of Scripture, from promise to fulfilment, followed honestly. Cut the text straight and it leads to a cross and an empty tomb, because that is where God laid the road.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only scholars can understand Scripture; its main message is clear to all (Psalm 19:7). Nor does rightly dividing (KJV) mean dividing Scripture into separate dispensations with different ways of salvation, as some have taught. The verb means cutting straight, handling correctly, as the ESV’s rightly handling shows. Paul is calling for accurate teaching of the whole word, not a scheme of divisions.

I am not a preacher. How do I handle the word rightly? Every Christian who reads the Bible, teaches a child, or shares a verse with a friend is handling it. Do it straight. Read whole passages, not isolated lines. Ask who wrote it, to whom, and why, before asking what it means for you. Let clear passages explain unclear ones. Notice how the passage points to Christ, for the whole Bible is about him (Luke 24:27). Be careful about lifting a promise made to someone else and claiming it unchanged. And when you do not understand something, say so, rather than forcing a meaning onto it. A plain, careful reading is far better than a clever, crooked one.

In a sentence. Make every effort to stand before God as someone tested and approved, a workman with nothing to be ashamed of, who handles the message of truth accurately.

On a Tuesday. When you read Scripture, read it carefully: in context, asking what it meant, then what it means. Ask God to make you an accurate handler of his word. This week, before quoting a verse to someone, read the whole chapter it comes from.

For worship. God has spoken, and his word is truth. He did not leave us to guess at him; he gave us a book in which every line is breathed out by him. And when the Son stood hungry in the wilderness and the devil quoted a psalm at him with a crooked cut, he answered with the word handled straight: it is written, and again, it is written (Matthew 4:1–11). The word held then, and it holds now. Blessed be the God who speaks, who makes the simple wise, and who will one day look at the work of his servants with the only approval that matters: well done.

verseByVerse.quote: But avoid irreverent babble, for it will lead people into more and more ungodliness, and their talk will spread like gangrene. Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have swerved from the truth, saying that the resurrection has already happened. They are upsetting the faith of some.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But avoid irreverent babble, for it will lead people into more and more ungodliness, and their talk will spread like gangrene. Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have swerved from the truth, saying that the resurrection has already happened. They are upsetting the faith of some.

But avoid irreverent babble. Not refute it: avoid it. “Avoid” (periistaso) is go around, shun, stand clear of. “Irreverent babble” (bebēlous kenophōnias) is godless empty chatter. It is the same instruction as 1 Timothy 6:20, and the same pastoral judgement: some error is not worth the dignity of an argument.

For it will lead people into more and more ungodliness. Then the reason, and it is a diagnosis of how error actually behaves. “Lead into more and more” (prokopsousin) is to advance, to make progress, and there is irony in it. The false teachers claimed to be making spiritual progress; they were progressing, but into ungodliness. Error does not settle at a tolerable level but leads on, and each position makes the next one thinkable. False doctrine never stands still; it gets worse.

And their talk will spread like gangrene. “Gangrene” (gangraina) is a spreading, eating sore: dead tissue that spreads and destroys healthy flesh. Paul, who has used the language of sound, healthy teaching throughout these letters, chooses the most unpleasant word available. Gangrene does not stay where it started, cannot be reasoned with, and is treated by cutting away. Error spreads by contact. False teaching is a disease that infects and kills.

Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus. Hymenaeus appeared in the first letter, handed over to Satan that he might learn not to blaspheme (1 Timothy 1:20). He is still at it, and has acquired a colleague; Philetus is otherwise unknown. Discipline had been applied and had not, so far, worked, which the New Testament records without pretending otherwise. They have swerved from the truth: “swerved” (ēstochēsan) is missed the mark, as in 1 Timothy 1:6 and 6:21. They were aiming at the target and are now nowhere near it.

Saying that the resurrection has already happened. Their error is specified. Almost certainly it was a spiritualising of the resurrection: that it means the new life a believer has now, experienced at conversion or baptism, and there is nothing bodily still to come. This probably came from a view that the body is unimportant or evil (1 Timothy 4:3). It is an attractive teaching, because it sounds advanced and requires nothing to be waited for. Paul had dealt with denial of the resurrection in Corinth (1 Corinthians 15:12), and it is a serious error: without a bodily resurrection, Christianity is destroyed (1 Corinthians 15:14–19).

They are upsetting the faith of some. “Upsetting” (anatrepousin) is overturning, subverting, as one overturns a table: the same idea as the ruin of verse 14. Real damage was being done, and this is precisely why it matters. If the resurrection has already happened, then the Christians whose bodies are in the ground have missed it, and everyone still suffering has nothing coming. It is the identical pastoral wreckage the Thessalonians suffered when told the day of the Lord had already come (2 Thessalonians 2:2), and both times it landed on the grieving first.

A resurrection with nail marks. The teachers were right that one resurrection has already happened, but it was not ours. It was Christ’s, and it was bodily: a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have, he told his frightened disciples, and he showed them his hands and his feet (Luke 24:39). Paul has just told Timothy to remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead (v. 8), and that is the answer to Hymenaeus. Christ rose as the firstfruits (1 Corinthians 15:20), and the firstfruits are the first sheaf of the same harvest. A risen body in the past guarantees risen bodies in the future. Spiritualise ours, and you have quietly spiritualised his.

Is full preterism the same error? Some today teach a similar error, full preterism, which holds that Christ’s return and the resurrection were fulfilled in AD 70. Paul’s verdict on Hymenaeus applies to it: to say the resurrection has already happened is to swerve from the truth and upset faith. The resurrection of the body is still to come.

What it does not mean. It does not deny that believers have already been raised with Christ spiritually (Ephesians 2:6; Colossians 3:1). That is true. The error is saying that is all there is, denying the future bodily resurrection.

How do I avoid error without becoming closed-minded? Being open to learning and being open to anything are different. Stay teachable: test what you hear by Scripture, and be willing to be corrected by it, even when that means changing your mind. But you need not give every new idea a hearing, any more than a doctor must try every remedy advertised online. Avoiding godless chatter means not feeding on it: not spending your evenings on teachers who sneer at the Bible or sell novelties, not letting curiosity lead you where you would not take your children. Know the truth well, and the counterfeit becomes easier to spot. Bank clerks learn to detect forgeries chiefly by handling the real thing.

In a sentence. But steer clear of godless, empty talk, because those who indulge in it will go further and further into ungodliness, and their teaching will spread like an eating sore. Hymenaeus and Philetus are among them; they have missed the truth by claiming that the resurrection has already taken place, and they are overturning some people’s faith.

On a Tuesday. Look at what you are feeding your mind on: podcasts, videos, books, conversations. Is any of it slowly turning you from the plain truth of Scripture? Cut away what is spreading. And if you know someone grieving whose hope has been shaken, remind them gently that the resurrection is still to come, and that it is a resurrection of the body.

For worship. The Lord Jesus did not leave his body in the tomb, and he will not leave ours there either. The hands that were pierced are still his hands, and the Spirit who raised him from the dead will give life to the mortal bodies of all who are his (Romans 8:11). The graves of the saints are not monuments to what is over but seed beds of what is coming: sown in weakness, raised in power, made like his glorious body. Blessed be the risen Christ, whose own scars are the pledge that nothing of his people will be lost, and who will swallow up death in victory.

verseByVerse.quote: But God's firm foundation stands, bearing this seal: "The Lord knows those who are his," and, "Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But God’s firm foundation stands, bearing this seal: “The Lord knows those who are his,” and, “Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity.”

But God’s firm foundation stands. Against men who are overturning the faith of some, Paul sets something that cannot be overturned. “Firm” (stereos) is solid, steadfast; “foundation” (themelios) is a building’s foundation stone. False teachers may overturn some people’s faith (v. 18), but they cannot overturn God’s foundation. The foundation is probably God’s church built on his truth (1 Timothy 3:15), or God’s saving work itself. And “stands” (hestēken) is perfect tense: has stood and continues standing.

Bearing this seal. “Seal” (sphragis). In the ancient world a foundation stone might bear an inscription indicating ownership and purpose, and a seal marked ownership and guaranteed authenticity. Paul says this one carries two inscriptions, and they face in opposite directions.

The Lord knows those who are his. The first inscription is God’s side. It echoes Moses’ words during the rebellion of Korah, when God showed who truly belonged to him (Numbers 16:5), and that is Timothy’s situation: respected teachers have defected and nobody is sure who is sound. The register is not kept by us. “Knows” (egnō) is more than awareness; it is God’s loving, electing knowledge, by which he chose and owns his people (John 10:14, 27; Romans 8:29; Galatians 4:9). When some fall away, the truly chosen remain. You may have been badly wrong about somebody. He is not in any doubt.

Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity. The second inscription is our side. It perhaps echoes the warning in the same story, to depart from the tents of the wicked men (Numbers 16:26), and Isaiah 52:11. “Names the name of the Lord” is to profess faith in Christ, to call on him. “Depart” (apostētō) is withdraw, turn away; “iniquity” (adikia) is unrighteousness. If you cannot verify who belongs to God, you can attend to your own conduct, and the standard is stated as a consequence of the naming. Whoever claims the name is thereby committed to leaving the sin. The evidence of belonging to God is turning from sin.

The name on the seal. For Paul, the Lord of both inscriptions is the Lord Jesus. To name the name of the Lord is to call on Jesus as Lord (Romans 10:9, 13), and the one who knows his own is the Good Shepherd, who knows his sheep and is known by them. So the seal bears his mark on both sides: he owns his people, and his people leave the sin he died to take away. And the foundation itself rests on him, for no one can lay a foundation other than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 3:11). Heretics can shake people standing in the building. They cannot touch the stone.

Two lines on one seal. Hold the two together and you have the balance the whole New Testament keeps. Assurance rests on God’s knowledge, not on our performance; nobody is kept by the quality of their departure from iniquity. And the evidence that a person belongs is precisely that departure. The seal has two lines, and a foundation with only one of them on it will not hold a building up.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God’s knowledge makes our holiness unnecessary. The two seals go together: God knows his own, and his own depart from iniquity. Election and holiness are inseparable (Ephesians 1:4; 2 Peter 1:10). Nor does it mean we can know infallibly who the elect are; we see the fruit.

Someone I trusted as a Christian has fallen away. Was I deceived, and could it happen to me? It may be that he was never truly the Lord’s, though he looked it (1 John 2:19); or it may be that he is a believer in a terrible fall, whom God will yet bring back. You cannot always tell, and you are not asked to. The Lord knows. As for you: the same seal that comforts also directs. Do not look for assurance in your own cleverness at spotting frauds, nor in your past experience alone, but in Christ, and in the fruit his Spirit is producing now: a love for him, a hatred of your sin, and a continuing turning from it. Those whom the Lord knows, he keeps (John 10:27–29).

In a sentence. Yet God’s solid foundation stands firm, stamped with these words: the Lord knows those who belong to him, and everyone who calls on the Lord’s name must turn away from wickedness.

On a Tuesday. When others fall away, take comfort: the Lord knows those who are his. Then attend to the second line: name one specific iniquity you are tolerating, and depart from it today, practically, by removing the access, making the call, or confessing to a friend.

For worship. The church has been shaken by heresy in every age, by Arius and Pelagius and a thousand lesser names, and the foundation has never moved. It does not stand on the reliability of its members; it stands on the knowledge of God, who wrote the names of his people in his book before the world began and has never lost a page. The Lord whose name is on the seal bought his people with his own blood, and he does not mislay what he has paid for. Blessed be the God who knows, whose seal is unbroken, and on whose foundation the weakest believer stands as firm as the apostle.
verseByVerse.note: The first saying echoes the rebellion of Korah; the second gathers the sense of Moses’ warning to leave the rebels’ tents.

parallels.desc: the LORD will show who is his
Depart, please, from the tents of these wicked men

verseByVerse.quote: Now in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver but also of wood and clay, some for honorable use, some for dishonorable. Therefore, if anyone cleanses himself from what is dishonorable, he will be a vessel for honorable use, set apart as holy, useful to the master of the house, ready for every good work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver but also of wood and clay, some for honorable use, some for dishonorable. Therefore, if anyone cleanses himself from what is dishonorable, he will be a vessel for honorable use, set apart as holy, useful to the master of the house, ready for every good work.

Now in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver but also of wood and clay. Paul stays with the house. A “great house” (megalē oikia) is a large household, a mansion, and the picture is a large establishment with a range of equipment. “Vessels” (skeuē) are utensils, containers, dishes. Gold and silver for the table; wood and clay for the kitchen, the yard, and the jobs nobody describes at dinner, the pots for rubbish and waste. Every big household had both, and nobody thought this strange.

Some for honorable use, some for dishonorable. “Honourable” (timē) is for use at the master’s table; “dishonourable” (atimia) is for menial or disgusting tasks. Applied to the church, the household of God (1 Timothy 3:15), it accounts for what Timothy is looking at. The visible church contains a mix of people. Hymenaeus and Philetus are in the house; in context they are the dishonourable vessels, and the honourable are faithful believers. Their presence does not mean the house is false; large households have always held vessels of very different kinds.

Therefore, if anyone cleanses himself from what is dishonorable. Then verse 21 makes the turn, and it is the crucial move. “Cleanses himself” (ekkathērē heauton) is purges himself thoroughly. “What is dishonourable” is literally from these (apo toutōn): from the false teachers and their teaching, and from the sin that goes with it. Notice what Paul does not say. He does not tell Timothy to sort the house or identify which people are the clay ones. The instruction is reflexive: cleanse yourself. Faced with a congregation containing frauds, the temptation is to spend your energy on auditing everybody else, and Paul redirects it entirely.

He will be a vessel for honorable use. The metaphor shifts, and the promise is remarkable, because it means the classification is not fixed. A vessel can move category. Nobody in this house is stuck being clay, and the transfer is effected by cleansing rather than by gifting or promotion.

The master who chose a persecutor. Paul knew this from his own life. On the Damascus road he was the most dishonourable article in the house, a persecutor of the church, and the Lord Jesus said of him to Ananias, he is a chosen instrument of mine, literally a vessel (skeuos), to carry my name (Acts 9:15). The master of this house is Christ, and the cleansing that makes a vessel fit for him begins with his washing, not ours (Titus 3:5). The vessel’s own cleansing is real, but it is the response of something already claimed by the master and wanted at his table.

Set apart as holy, useful to the master of the house, ready for every good work. “Set apart as holy” (hēgiasmenon) is a perfect tense: consecrated for God’s use and remaining so. “Useful” (euchrēston) is serviceable to the master (despotēs), the owner. “Ready” (hētoimasmenon) is prepared and available for whatever he requires (3:17). The middle word is the plainest ambition in Scripture: not admired, not prominent, but useful. The whole point of being clean is that you can be used without spoiling what is put in you.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we save ourselves by cleansing ourselves; we are washed by Christ (1 Corinthians 6:11). It means believers, enabled by grace, must actively separate from error and sin in order to be fit for service (Philippians 2:12–13). Nor does it mean the church can ever be perfectly pure in this age; there will always be a mix (Matthew 13:24–30).

Should I leave a church that has false teachers in it? It depends on where the error is and what the church does about it. Every church has weak and sinful members, and you should not leave because the house contains clay pots; neither did Timothy. Your first duty is to cleanse yourself, and to pray and speak up through proper channels. But if the leaders themselves teach a different gospel, deny essential truths such as the resurrection, or refuse to deal with open error, then the church is no longer feeding you or your family safely, and it is right to seek a faithful one (Galatians 1:8–9). Leave graciously, without gossip, and if possible explain your reasons to the elders.

How do I cleanse myself in practice? By turning from what defiles and coming to Christ who washes. Name the specific things: a habit, a source of false teaching you listen to, a relationship that is pulling you into sin. Confess them to God, receiving his forgiveness (1 John 1:9). Then cut off the supply, as Jesus said, if your eye causes you to sin (Matthew 5:29–30). Replace it with what is good (Philippians 4:8). This is not self-salvation; it is the Spirit at work in you, and you do it because you have been washed, not in order to be.

In a sentence. In a large house there are not only gold and silver dishes but also wooden and earthenware ones, some for special occasions and some for menial use. So if anyone keeps himself clean from what is dishonourable, he will be a vessel for special use, set apart, useful to the master, and ready for every good task.

On a Tuesday. What do you need to cleanse yourself from to be more useful to Christ? Confess it and turn from it today. Then offer yourself to him for whatever he wants this week, the small, unseen jobs included, and see what he puts in your hands.

For worship. The Master of the house does not need us, and yet he chooses to use us. He takes clay and makes it holy; he washes what was soiled and sets it on his own table. The Lord Jesus himself took the form of a servant, a vessel emptied and poured out, and through his blood the most dishonourable of us can be made clean and useful. Blessed be the God who makes beautiful things out of the dust, who fills earthen vessels with his glory, and who will one day show to all the house what he has made of the least of his servants.

verseByVerse.quote: So flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace, along with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace, along with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart.

So flee youthful passions. “Flee” (pheuge) is run from, as in 1 Timothy 6:11, and it is paired with the next verb: run from, and run toward. “Youthful passions” (neōterikas epithymias) certainly include sexual desire; Timothy was a young man, told to treat younger women as sisters, in all purity (1 Timothy 5:2). But the next verse is about quarrels, and the passions of a young man also include the appetite for argument, the need to be proved right, impatience, pride, the desire for novelty and the ambition to make a mark quickly. A young minister facing Hymenaeus and Philetus will be tempted to take them on and win, and Paul lists that instinct among the things to run from.

And pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace. “Pursue” (diōke) is chase. The four to chase are worth their order: righteousness, right living and right dealing; faith, trust and faithfulness; love; and peace, harmony, the opposite of the quarrels in verses 14 and 23. Peace is the pointed one in a chapter about word-fights.

The four are found in Christ. The things Timothy is told to chase are not abstract virtues. They are what he already has in Christ, worked out in his life. Christ Jesus became to us righteousness from God (1 Corinthians 1:30); he is the one in whom faith rests; his love surpasses knowledge (Ephesians 3:19); and he himself is our peace (Ephesians 2:14). To pursue them is to become in practice what we already are in him, and so, in the end, to chase a person. That is why the pursuit is hopeful. Timothy is not running after something he may never reach, but growing into the likeness of the one who has already made him his own (Philippians 3:12).

Along with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart. This clause is easy to skip and is the most practical thing in the verse: the pursuit is not solo. Timothy is to run in company, and the company is specified: those who call on the Lord (epikaloumenōn ton kyrion), genuine believers who worship and pray to Christ (Romans 10:13; 1 Corinthians 1:2), from a pure heart, sincere, not hypocritical (1 Timothy 1:5). Paul’s answer to a young man surrounded by corrosive people is not isolation but better company, and separation from false teachers (v. 21) goes together with fellowship with true believers. You cannot always choose your congregation, but you can largely choose whom you spend your time with inside it, and over ten years that choice shapes a person more than almost anything else.

What it does not mean. It does not mean youth is sinful or that young people cannot be godly; Timothy himself was an example (1 Timothy 4:12). Nor does it mean we pursue holiness in isolation.

I am not young any more. Does this verse still apply? Yes. Youthful passions are typical of youth, but they do not check your birth certificate. Many older believers still crave the last word, still flare up when contradicted, still chase novelty, still struggle with lust. And age has its own temptations: bitterness, a hardened opinion, a love of comfort. The command is the same at every age: run from the sin that is characteristic of your season of life, and chase righteousness, faith, love and peace with others who love the Lord. An older believer who has learned to flee and pursue is exactly the companion a younger one needs.

What if I cannot find such companions? Pray for them, and look harder than you have. They are often quieter than the loudest people in a church: the faithful at the prayer meeting, the older couple who have walked with God for decades, the young believer who is hungry for Scripture. Take the first step: invite one person to read the Bible and pray with you. Be the kind of companion you are looking for. If your church truly has none, that may be a sign to seek a healthier one. And remember you are never entirely alone; the Lord himself walks with those who call on him.

In a sentence. So run from the desires that drive the young, and pursue righteousness, faith, love and peace, together with all who call on the Lord with a clean heart.

On a Tuesday. Who are you pursuing godliness with? Find one or two believers to pray with and encourage regularly. And name the youthful passion you most need to flee this week, whether lust, argument, impatience or ambition, and decide in advance what you will do instead when it rises.

For worship. Christ was a young man too, about thirty when his ministry began, and he met every passion of youth without once falling: tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin. He never needed the last word, though he is the Word; he never grasped at a name, though his is the name above every name. And he did not run alone; he chose twelve, and called them friends. Blessed be the Saviour who runs ahead of us and beside us, and who will present us blameless before the presence of his glory.

verseByVerse.quote: Have nothing to do with foolish, ignorant controversies; you know that they breed quarrels. And the Lord's servant must not be quarrelsome but kind to everyone, able to teach, patiently enduring evil, correcting his opponents with gentleness. God may perhaps grant them repentance leading to a knowledge of the truth, and they may come to their senses and escape from the snare of the devil, after being captured by him to do his will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Have nothing to do with foolish, ignorant controversies; you know that they breed quarrels. And the Lord’s servant must not be quarrelsome but kind to everyone, able to teach, patiently enduring evil, correcting his opponents with gentleness. God may perhaps grant them repentance leading to a knowledge of the truth, and they may come to their senses and escape from the snare of the devil, after being captured by him to do his will.

Have nothing to do with foolish, ignorant controversies. “Have nothing to do with” (paraitou) is refuse, decline. “Foolish” (mōras) is stupid, the word that gives us moron. “Ignorant” (apaideutous) is uneducated, undisciplined, ill-informed. “Controversies” (zētēseis) are speculative questions.

You know that they breed quarrels. “Breed” (gennōsin) is a birth word, give birth to. Controversies do not merely lead to quarrels (machas, fights, battles); they generate them, and they keep doing it. “You know” is Paul’s way of saying this is not a theory. Timothy has watched it happen, and could have predicted the outcome.

And the Lord’s servant must not be quarrelsome. Then the portrait of the alternative, and it is one of the finest descriptions of a Christian teacher anywhere. “The Lord’s servant” (doulon kyriou) is the Lord’s slave, a title used of Moses, David and the prophets, here for Timothy and every minister. “Must not be quarrelsome” (ou dei machesthai) is must not fight, the same requirement as an overseer (1 Timothy 3:3).

But kind to everyone. “Kind” (ēpion) is gentle, mild, the word used of a nursing mother (1 Thessalonians 2:7). To everyone, and the scope includes the opponents.

Able to teach, patiently enduring evil. “Able to teach” (didaktikon), as in 1 Timothy 3:2, is the one skill on the overseer’s list, and it sits between two dispositions rather than standing alone. The answer to error is not fighting but teaching. “Patiently enduring evil” is a single word (anexikakon): bearing wrong without resentment, taking hostility without retaliating. It assumes he will be ill-treated.

Correcting his opponents with gentleness. Both halves at once. “Correcting” (paideuonta) is instructing, training, disciplining; the word means instructing so as to change someone. He does correct: this is not a counsel of vagueness. “Opponents” (antidiatithemenous) are those who set themselves against him. And he does it with gentleness (prautēs, meekness, humility, mildness), not harshly, sarcastically or arrogantly. Most of us can manage one or the other.

God may perhaps grant them repentance. Then the reason, and it changes the whole temperature. “Grant” (dōē) is give. Repentance is God’s gift (Acts 5:31; 11:18). That is why gentleness is not weakness or mere good manners. If the outcome depended on the teacher’s argument, then overwhelming force would be the sensible tactic. It does not. A man cannot argue anybody into the kingdom, so his job is to correct clearly, treat people well, and leave the granting to God. “Perhaps” (mēpote): we do not know to whom God will grant repentance, but we hope and pray. And it leads to a knowledge of the truth (epignōsis, full knowledge), for repentance and right belief go together (3:7; 1 Timothy 2:4).

And they may come to their senses. “Come to their senses” (ananēpsōsin) is become sober again, wake up from drunkenness. The verb suggests a man sobering up. False teaching is like intoxication; it clouds the mind.

And escape from the snare of the devil, after being captured by him to do his will. “Snare” (pagis) is a trap. “Captured” (ezōgrēmenoi) is taken alive, captured as prisoners of war. Paul’s picture of his opponents is not that they are villains but that they are caught: taken alive in a trap, held, doing somebody else’s will while believing it is their own. Grammatically, his will could refer to the devil’s will or God’s will; most take it as the devil’s. That is how Paul sees the men wrecking his churches, and it is why he tells Timothy to be gentle with them.

The stronger man. Gentleness toward captives would be naive if the captor were undefeated. He is not. Jesus said that no one can enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man (Mark 3:27), and at the cross he disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame (Colossians 2:15). Everyone who comes to their senses and walks out of the devil’s trap is plunder taken back by a stronger hand. That is why the Lord’s servant can afford to be patient. He is not breaking the snare by the force of his own argument; he is speaking the word through which the risen Christ still frees his prisoners.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ministers should never be firm or never confront error. Paul is firm throughout. It means confrontation is done with gentleness, patience and hope. Nor does God may grant repentance mean human response is not real; people do repent, but they repent because God grants it.

Are people in error to blame if the devil has captured them? Yes. Captivity here is not an excuse; they are opponents of the truth, and they must repent, which means turning from something they are responsible for. But it is a reason for compassion. Before God called us, we too were following the prince of the power of the air (Ephesians 2:1–3), and we were freed not by our cleverness but by grace. So the person who opposes you is not your real enemy; he is a prisoner of your real enemy (Ephesians 6:12). Hate the trap, pity the captive, and pray for the God who sets prisoners free.

Does gentleness mean I must keep arguing with someone forever? No. Gentleness governs how you correct, not how long. Paul himself says to have nothing to do with foolish controversies (v. 23), and elsewhere to warn a divisive person once and then twice, and after that have nothing more to do with him (Titus 3:10). You may decline a debate that has become a quarrel, end a conversation kindly, or refuse to keep feeding someone who only wants to fight. What you may not do is become harsh, sarcastic or contemptuous. Say what is true, say it kindly, pray, and leave the outcome with God.

In a sentence. Refuse to get involved in foolish and ill-informed arguments; you know they only produce fights. The Lord’s servant must not be a fighter but must be gentle with everyone, able to teach, patient when wronged, correcting those who oppose him with humility. Perhaps God will give them repentance so that they come to know the truth, and they will come to their senses and get free from the devil’s trap, where he has held them captive to do his will.

On a Tuesday. Think of someone who opposes the truth. Pray for God to grant them repentance, and speak to them gently next time you have the chance. If you correct anyone this week, a child, a colleague, a fellow church member, check your tone first: would they hear in it that you want their good?

For worship. This is how God dealt with us. We were opponents, captives of the devil, drunk on our own wisdom, and he did not overwhelm us with force. He sent his Son, gentle and lowly in heart, who endured the hostility of sinners, did not revile when he was reviled, and prayed for those who crucified him. Then he granted us repentance and woke us up. Every believer is a captive set free and a drunkard made sober. Glory to the God who grants repentance, who breaks the snare of the fowler, and whose kindness leads the hardest heart home.
